column1: Telegram setMyCommands: what's the unit of a command list, and how does it update?
column2:
Unit = a {scope, language_code} PAIR — each is independent, own 100-cmd limit.
setMyCommands OVERWRITES that pair's whole list (no partial update; [] clears it).
So one 'chat scope in 4 languages' = 4 independent setMyCommands calls.

column1: Telegram: you set a chat menu in 4 languages — how do you fully remove it?
column2:
deleteMyCommands ALSO targets one {scope, language_code} pair. A single delete
(no language_code) clears only the default entry — the ru/uk/en lists survive.
Removal must MIRROR the set: loop the same LOCALES and deleteMyCommands per language.

Most-specific first: chat -> all_private_chats -> default
(within each, language-specific before language-agnostic).
=> deleting a chat-scoped list makes the chat FALL BACK to all_private_chats.
So clearing a manager's chat scope reverts them to the public menu automatically.

column1: Guard smell: when is `if (!x)` wrong for a `T | null` return?
column2:
When x can legitimately be a falsy value (0, "", false). !x fires on ALL of them,
not just null. Match the guard to the function's actual sentinel:
  parseChatId returns number | null  ->  if (x === null), NOT if (!x)  (0 is a valid id).

column1: Where does Telegram/edge work go: handler or service?
column2:
Handler = the EDGE: has ctx / ctx.api / ctx.reply, talks to Telegram & the outside world.
Service = the CORE: Prisma-only data logic, no ctx, doesn't know Telegram exists; returns a token.
=> setting a command scope (a Telegram concern) lives in the HANDLER, never the service.
Waiter (handler) carries orders; kitchen (service) just cooks.
